# The AI-Native Design Life Cycle {#sec-architecture-20-ontology}

::: {.epigraph}
> "All models are wrong but some are useful."
>
> — George E. P. Box, *Robustness in the Strategy of Scientific Model Building* [@Box1979Robustness, p. 202]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *Once an AI-native design system is being considered, how should the design work be organized, and why does that structure matter?*

**Core thesis:** *An explicit life cycle connects architectural intent to a reviewed decision. Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit answer distinct questions, and each stage can send work back for revision as the team learns about the design.*
:::

Generative AI models and automated search tools can draft register-transfer level (RTL) code, compiler schedules, and microarchitectural configurations. Turning a proposal into a useful architecture result requires a longer chain of work. A simulated throughput gain can disappear when physical timing fails. Repeated tool runs help little unless the team can tell whether to revise the hardware, repair the tool setup, or reconsider an assumption. The six-stage life cycle in @fig-ch03-cover-map separates these responsibilities while keeping the question, candidates, and evidence connected across iterations.

Evaluation determines which requirements a candidate satisfies, while interpretation tests explanations for its behavior and points to the work that needs revision. A study record ties those revisions and their results to the original question, baseline, and comparison conditions. It keeps failed attempts and unresolved limits in view so that the responsible architect can decide whether to advance, reject, revise, or stop.

In our constructed neural processing unit (NPU) accumulator study, a centralized candidate's timing failure motivates diagnostic tests and a possible banked revision. That revision still requires implementation and checking before it can support a recommendation. The example illustrates how feedback guides further design work within our prospective Lighthouse system-on-chip (SoC), the wearable design challenge of @sec-intent-vs-spec; it reports no executed Lighthouse result.

![**Six life-cycle stages connect architectural intent to a reviewed decision through explicit handoffs.** Each stage produces a distinct deliverable: a scoped plan, legal candidates, an execution record, a checked comparison, a supported causal account, and a decision to advance, revise, reject, or stop. Targeted repair aims to route a failure back to the stage that owns the broken assumption or artifact without discarding valid earlier work.](images/ch03-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch03-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which six life-cycle activities run from formulation through review and decision. Feedback returns work to earlier activities for investigation and revision."}

## What Breaks Without a Structured Life Cycle {#sec-unstructured-loop-failures}

When a team first brings a generative AI model or search algorithm into hardware development, the most tempting setup is an unscripted loop. The model proposes an RTL block or parameter change, a simulator or synthesis script runs it, and any error log goes straight back into the prompt until the script exits cleanly. On a standalone arithmetic kernel, that informal cycle feels responsive. On a real subsystem under tight power and timing budgets, we expect the same loop to turn rapid iteration into compounding confusion, because nothing separates problem definition from exploration, implementation, and evaluation. The failure modes below are what we anticipate from how these tools and prompts work; no study in this chapter compares a staged life cycle against an unstructured loop.

The first casualty of an unstructured loop is the baseline itself. When a candidate NPU accumulator misses its throughput or clock target after several automated edits, an unconstrained workflow has no rule separating fixed problem assumptions from choices the generator is free to vary. Across successive retries, a language model or engineer can quietly alter the workload trace, relax a pipeline latency target, or swap a cycle-accurate memory model for an idealized zero-delay stub just to get a clean run. After a few dozen iterations, the loop is still producing latency and area tables. No one can tell, however, whether the latest candidate is genuinely faster than the original baseline or merely evaluated under softer conditions.

Even when the workload stays fixed, coupling generation directly to evaluation lets an automated loop silence a failing check rather than fix the hardware. If a proposed crossbar organization fails timing analysis or triggers a testbench assertion, an automated agent with write access to the run directory can satisfy its immediate prompt by widening the clock period in the timing-constraint file, marking the critical path as a false path, or weakening the testbench check. The tool script returns zero errors, yet the underlying silicon violation remains untouched.

Finally, an unstructured loop cannot tell one late failure from another. A lint or synthesis error points directly to the offending RTL line, but a setup violation found at timing signoff arrives as a failing path through a gate-level netlist. That path, evaluated with extracted wire resistance and capacitance across several process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners,[^fn-pvt-c03] sits far from the architectural choice that produced it. The shortfall might stem from an unrealistic clock target set at the start of the study, a wide crossbar topology that cannot route cleanly, or a misconfigured analysis script, and each cause calls for a different repair. Without stage boundaries that keep those causes distinct, every failure feeds the same generic retry prompt. The loop then launches new RTL variants into long physical implementation runs and fills tool queues with unexamined candidates, when the real fix was to revise an upstream assumption or repair a broken script.

## The Six Stages of the AI-Native Life Cycle {#sec-arch2-ontology}

Reducing those anticipated failures calls for an organized path from an initial design idea to an engineering commitment, one in which what the team learns at each step informs the others without corrupting the baseline. Separating requirements, design alternatives, implementation, and verification has deep roots in systems engineering, where these activities remain iterative and interdependent [@NASA2017SystemsEngineeringHandbook, chaps. 4–5]. The six stages used here organize recurring architecture work so that an engineer can follow a candidate design, see what its measurements actually establish, and identify what needs to change when a check fails.

Existing project milestones such as RTL freeze and timing signoff remain in place; the six stages describe the design work that recurs before and between them. A stage marks a position in the forward sequence, but the team can return to it whenever later work exposes a problem that the stage owns. A failing timing check may therefore send the team back to Formulate to reconsider the clock target, Explore to revise the microarchitecture, or Implement to fix the tool setup, without discarding valid intermediate work.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Isolate failure domains for repair"}
**The principle:** Separate design activities so that a failed result can be traced to the assumptions, artifacts, or checks that need revision.

**The application:** Use the available diagnostics to choose what to revisit, preserving earlier work whose assumptions still hold. When the cause is uncertain or spans several activities, investigate it before choosing a repair.
:::

Each stage answers a question that the next activity depends on:

1. **Formulate.** What should the design achieve? State the question, baseline, constraints, permitted changes, and checks that will judge the result.
2. **Explore.** What alternatives are worth testing? Generate or select candidates, including different hardware and software organizations when the question permits them.
3. **Implement.** How can each candidate be tested? Develop the required models, RTL, and software, and run the tools needed to examine them.
4. **Evaluate.** What do the results establish? Check that the observations are valid for the intended comparison, then determine which requirements are satisfied or still unresolved.
5. **Interpret.** Why did the design behave this way? Test explanations for gains and failures, and use what is learned to guide further design work.
6. **Commit.** What should happen next? Review the study and decide whether to advance a candidate, reject it, revise the study, or stop.

Prediction, generation, and optimization serve these stages as methods rather than adding stages of their own. The three operational layers of @sec-three-operational-layers, which differ in the design decisions an automated workflow may revisit, govern how much of this work may proceed automatically. A Layer 1 model might draft RTL during Implement or summarize a timing report during Interpret while engineers choose the next action. A Layer 2 optimizer can carry candidates through repeated tool runs within its prescribed template $\Theta$, a parameterized design family that architects fix before search begins, varying only its parameters $\theta \in \Theta$. A Layer 3 system may also revise the template itself within the study's authorized scope, using physical feedback to propose and test a new hardware organization and matching software. Whether that broader capability improves the result or reduces total cost remains an open question (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect).

Suppose one candidate Lighthouse design uses an NPU for part of its extended-reality (XR) workload, one of the compute options left open in @sec-moonshot. Our walkthrough focuses on the accumulator block that combines partial products into matrix-multiplication results. It asks how to improve that block's throughput within its allocated timing and power limits in a 3\ nm-class design flow. Although the candidates, timing failure, and diagnosis are constructed teaching examples, following this single block through @fig-ontology-loop shows how the six stages and their return paths operate inside a concrete investigation.

![**A scoped architecture study closes the loop only when empirical results drive the next action.** Forward execution steps from declaring the study plan and stopping conditions (Stage 1) through candidate generation, tool execution, measurement validation, and causal testing to a reviewed decision (Stages 2–6). When checked results call the original targets or constraints into question, the return path from Commit reopens Formulate to revise the study plan.](images/fig-ontology-loop){#fig-ontology-loop width="80%" fig-alt="Life-cycle diagram of six stages arranged in two rows, with arrows from Formulate through Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, to Commit. One return arrow leads from the decision back to formulation."}

A bounded architecture question like the NPU accumulator defines a *scoped study*, which investigates one part of the machine without claiming to settle the whole processor. Within that study, the work forms a design loop in the sense of @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales only when its results choose the next action, unlike a fixed parameter sweep.

Scoped studies also depend on one another across hierarchy levels. A subsystem study sets the NPU block's power and timing allocations within the Lighthouse subsystem's 3\ W envelope, while the block study tests whether those allocations can sustain a viable accumulator organization. If the tested candidates fail to close timing, the team may need to revisit the subsystem allocation or authorize further exploration; those failures alone do not establish that the allocation is impossible. The walkthrough traces this block study through all six stages before returning to the dependencies between coupled studies.

### Stage 1: Formulating the Architecture Question

Suppose a team sets out to "improve NPU accumulator throughput" without first fixing its baseline memory assumptions and interface rules. An automated search can then spend days optimizing an apparent accumulator bottleneck that vanishes once realistic bus contention is included, or propose a wider interface that breaks the surrounding SoC contract. Formulation is meant to reduce those wasted runs by turning a broad product goal into a testable comparison against an explicit baseline. For the NPU block, the question becomes concrete: can an alternative organization process more matrix-multiplication results per unit time than the baseline accumulator while meeting the target clock period, required numerical behavior, and allocated area and power budgets within the Lighthouse subsystem's 3\ W envelope? To answer it reliably, the team states the reference design, workload phases, memory and tool assumptions, and verification checks up front, and separates fixed system contracts from the choices the study is free to vary.

That boundary between fixed contracts and open choices also defines how far automated repair may reach. In the NPU accumulator walkthrough, the study may modify the internal datapath organization, pipeline structure, and supporting software schedule while holding external bus interfaces and numerical accuracy fixed. If downstream physical checks show that the bus protocol itself limits throughput, the repair loop cannot alter that protocol on its own and must return the question to the architect. Together with an explicit run budget and stopping criteria, these rules yield a testable question and an execution plan against which Explore can propose candidates.

### Stage 2: Exploring Candidate Designs

Once Formulate establishes the question and permitted changes, exploration develops candidate designs worth implementing. In the centralized NPU candidate, a crossbar routes outputs from parallel arithmetic units to shared storage and adders that hold and update partial sums. Alternatives include widening that crossbar, changing its pipeline structure, or distributing the partial sums among accumulator banks with local reduction trees, networks of adders that combine contributions near each bank. The software schedule must assign matrix tiles and their accumulation work to match where the partial sums reside; a schedule inherited from the centralized design may direct concurrent updates to the same bank while other banks sit idle. An optimizer can select among these alternatives only if its template already encodes them; proposing an organization outside that template requires broader design authority.

These alternatives trade off more than raw throughput. Adding parallel datapaths consumes extra storage and routing tracks, whereas banking can shorten critical interconnect wires at the cost of potential bank conflicts or extra reduction stages. Exploration surfaces these trade-offs and selects informative candidates to test rather than certifying physical feasibility from a high-level model. A cycle simulator that omits interconnect wire delay[^fn-wire-delay-c03] can overstate the throughput of a wider centralized crossbar because it ignores the resistance and capacitance of long wires. For the first pass through our walkthrough, suppose this high-level estimate makes the wider centralized candidate worth implementing. Banking remains an alternative to revisit if physical checks contradict that estimate.

[^fn-wire-delay-c03]: **Interconnect wire delay**: A 2001 projection across feature sizes from 180\ nm to 35\ nm found that local wires, which shorten with scaling, keep pace with gate delay or slow only gradually, whereas global wires fall behind gates even with repeaters [@HoMaiHorowitz2001FutureOfWires]. Depending on wire length and the target clock period, long interconnect wires across wide crossbars may need repeater buffers or pipelined traversal. A model that assumes single-cycle communication can then overestimate the implementation's throughput.

How a team searches those trade-offs depends on what limits the study. When only a few accumulator organizations are on the table, implementing and comparing them directly is often the cheapest path; a larger candidate space may justify predictive screening, optimization, or generation, each worth its setup cost only if it answers the comparison within the budget (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization).

```{python}
#| echo: false
import csv as _csv3ka
import json as _json3ka
from pathlib import Path as _Path3ka
import re as _re3ka
import _python.plots as _ap3ka

_ka10_dir = _Path3ka(_ap3ka.__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "data" / "studies" / "10-kernelagent-search"
_ka10_sum = {r["label"]: r for r in _json3ka.loads((_ka10_dir / "summary.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))}
_ka10_rows = list(_csv3ka.DictReader((_ka10_dir / "timings.csv").open(encoding="utf-8")))
ka10_tasks = len(_ka10_sum)
ka10_rounds = max(int(r["round"]) for r in _ka10_rows)
ka10_mv_ratio = f"{_ka10_sum['Matrix–vector']['first_over_best']:.2f}"
ka10_mv_best_round = _ka10_sum["Matrix–vector"]["best_round"]
ka10_rms_ratio = f"{_ka10_sum['RMSNorm']['first_over_best']:.2f}"

# Largest rise above the earlier low in the matrix–vector per-round records.
_ka10_mv = [float(r["time_ms"]) for r in _ka10_rows if r["label"] == "Matrix–vector"]
_ka10_rise = {i: _ka10_mv[i] / min(_ka10_mv[:i]) for i in range(1, len(_ka10_mv))}
_ka10_peak = max(_ka10_rise, key=_ka10_rise.get)
ka10_mv_low_round = _ka10_peak  # Rounds count from 1, so index i - 1 is round i.
ka10_mv_low_ms = f"{min(_ka10_mv[:_ka10_peak]):.2f}"
ka10_mv_peak_round = _ka10_peak + 1
ka10_mv_peak_ms = f"{_ka10_mv[_ka10_peak]:.2f}"
ka10_mv_peak_ratio = f"{_ka10_rise[_ka10_peak]:.2f}"

# The source's torch.compile baseline, read from its summary table.
_ka10_src = (_ka10_dir / "raw" / "README.md").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
_ka10_cmp = {
    int(k): (float(c), float(b))
    for k, c, b in _re3ka.findall(
        r"^\| `(\d+)_[^`]*` \| ([\d.]+) \| \*\*([\d.]+)\*\* \|", _ka10_src, _re3ka.M
    )
}
_ka10_mv_input = float(_re3ka.search(r"`input kernel`: \*\*([\d.]+)ms", _ka10_src).group(1))
ka10_mv_input_vs_compile = f"{_ka10_mv_input / _ka10_cmp[4][0]:.2f}"
ka10_mv_r1_vs_compile = f"{_ka10_sum['Matrix–vector']['first_ms'] / _ka10_cmp[4][0]:.2f}"
ka10_mv_vs_compile = f"{_ka10_cmp[4][0] / _ka10_cmp[4][1]:.2f}"
ka10_rms_vs_compile = f"{_ka10_cmp[36][0] / _ka10_cmp[36][1]:.2f}"

# Per-round records against the source's summary table.
_ka10_xc = _json3ka.loads((_ka10_dir / "readme_crosscheck.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
_ka10_off = [r for r in _ka10_xc if not r["matches_readme_to_three_decimals"]]
ka10_off_tasks = ("zero", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five")[len(_ka10_off)]
_ka10_max = max(_ka10_off, key=lambda r: abs(r["relative_difference_percent"]))
_ka10_tc = [float(v.strip(" *")) for v in _re3ka.search(
    r"### 77.*?\| Best \(ms\) \|(.*?)\|\n", _ka10_src, _re3ka.S).group(1).split("|")]
_ka10_tc_raw = [float(r["lowest_recorded_ms"]) for r in _ka10_rows if r["problem"] == _ka10_max["problem"]]
_ka10_tc_scale = [a / b for a, b in zip(_ka10_tc, _ka10_tc_raw)]
assert max(_ka10_tc_scale) - min(_ka10_tc_scale) < 0.01  # Near-constant factor across rounds.
ka10_tc_scale = f"{_ka10_tc_scale[-1]:.2f}"

# Attempt histories parsed from the source's prompts by reproduce.py.
_ka10_att = list(_csv3ka.DictReader((_ka10_dir / "attempts.csv").open(encoding="utf-8")))
_ka10_timed = [r for r in _ka10_att if r["time_ms"]]
ka10_hist_last_round = max(int(r["round"]) for r in _ka10_att)
ka10_mv_worst_ms = f"{max(float(r['time_ms']) for r in _ka10_timed if r['label'] == 'Matrix–vector'):.0f}"
ka10_tc_worst_ms = f"{max(float(r['time_ms']) for r in _ka10_timed if r['label'] == 'Transposed conv. 3D'):.0f}"
_ka10_mv_att = [r for r in _ka10_timed if r["label"] == "Matrix–vector"]
_ka10_spread = {k: v["round_1_start_spread"] for k, v in _ka10_sum.items()}
assert max(_ka10_spread, key=_ka10_spread.get) == "RMSNorm"  # The prose names the widest sample.
ka10_mv_start_spread = f"{_ka10_spread['Matrix–vector']:.2f}"
ka10_rms_start_spread = f"{_ka10_spread['RMSNorm']:.2f}"
ka10_mp_start_spread = f"{_ka10_spread['MaxPool 3D']:.2f}"
ka10_conv_start_spread = f"{_ka10_spread['Transposed conv. 3D']:.2f}"
assert ka10_conv_start_spread == f"{_ka10_spread['Depthwise conv. 2D']:.2f}"  # One value stands for both.
_ka10_peak_att = [r for r in _ka10_mv_att if int(r["round"]) == ka10_mv_peak_round]
_ka10_parent = float(min(_ka10_peak_att, key=lambda r: float(r["time_ms"]))["baseline_ms"])
ka10_mv_parent_ms = f"{_ka10_parent:.2f}"
ka10_mv_parent_ratio = f"{_ka10_mv[_ka10_peak] / _ka10_parent:.2f}"
_ka10_from_low = [float(r["time_ms"]) for r in _ka10_peak_att if abs(float(r["baseline_ms"]) - min(_ka10_mv[:_ka10_peak])) < 1e-3]
_ka10_from_low_mean = sum(_ka10_from_low) / len(_ka10_from_low)
ka10_mv_from_low_ms = f"{_ka10_from_low_mean:.0f}"
_ka10_from_low_ratio = _ka10_from_low_mean / min(_ka10_mv[:_ka10_peak])
ka10_mv_from_low_ratio = f"{_ka10_from_low_ratio:.1f}"
assert _ka10_mv[_ka10_peak] / _ka10_parent < _ka10_spread["RMSNorm"] < _ka10_from_low_ratio  # The prose orders these three.
ka10_mv_other_rise = f"{max(v for k, v in _ka10_rise.items() if k != _ka10_peak):.2f}"

# Base rates across all five tasks, judged against the widest replicate spread.
_ka10_widest = max(_ka10_spread.values())
_ka10_steps = [float(r["time_ms"]) / float(r["baseline_ms"]) for r in _ka10_timed]
ka10_att_timed = len(_ka10_steps)
ka10_att_slower = sum(v > 1 for v in _ka10_steps)
ka10_att_faster = sum(v < 1 for v in _ka10_steps)
assert ka10_att_slower + ka10_att_faster == ka10_att_timed
ka10_att_slower_beyond = sum(v > _ka10_widest for v in _ka10_steps)
ka10_att_faster_beyond = sum(1 / v > _ka10_widest for v in _ka10_steps)
_ka10_by_task = {}
for _r in _ka10_rows:
    _ka10_by_task.setdefault(_r["label"], []).append(float(_r["time_ms"]))
_ka10_late = [(k, v[i] / min(v[:i])) for k, v in _ka10_by_task.items() for i in range(1, len(v))]
ka10_late_rounds = len(_ka10_late)
ka10_late_above = sum(x > 1 for _, x in _ka10_late)
ka10_late_beyond = sum(x > _ka10_widest for _, x in _ka10_late)
assert {k for k, x in _ka10_late if x > _ka10_widest} == set(_ka10_by_task) - {"RMSNorm"}  # The prose names the exception.
_ka10_rms = _ka10_sum["RMSNorm"]
assert _ka10_rms["final_kernel_round"] != _ka10_rms["best_round"]  # The prose separates kept from lowest.
ka10_rms_final_round = _ka10_rms["final_kernel_round"]
ka10_rms_low_round = _ka10_rms["best_round"]
ka10_rms_final_gap_pct = f"{100 * (_ka10_rms['final_kernel_round_ms'] / _ka10_rms['best_ms'] - 1):.2f}"
ka10_warmup_records = _ka10_rows[0]["warmup"]
ka10_warmup_script = _re3ka.search(
    r"^WARMUP_ITERS = (\d+)", (_ka10_dir / "raw" / "benchmark.py").read_text(encoding="utf-8"), _re3ka.M
).group(1)
```

Whichever method proposes the candidates, the exploration history records why each one was selected or set aside, including failed trials that may guide later choices. Publicly released KernelAgent traces [@Cheng2025KernelAgentArtifacts] show what the lowest recorded time leaves out (@fig-ch03-kernelagent-search-trajectories). In this bounded kernel search, a round's recorded candidate can run slower than the lowest time recorded so far, even while later rounds lower that time.

![**Per-round best times can rise while the lowest recorded time falls.** Traces of `{python} ka10_tasks` curated KernelBench operators over `{python} ka10_rounds` rounds of four beam-search workers [@Cheng2025KernelAgentArtifacts]: (a) matrix–vector multiplication per-round best time (dashed line, joining separate beam branches, not one lineage) and lowest recorded time so far (solid step curve), which falls `{python} ka10_mv_ratio`$\times$ from Round 1 to Round `{python} ka10_mv_best_round`; and (b) lowest recorded time relative to Round 1, where RMSNorm stays nearly flat. Round 1 is itself a search output, and the source's `torch.compile` baseline reverses that contrast. Times are single reported values, not independently rerun.](images/fig-ch03-kernelagent-search-trajectories){#fig-ch03-kernelagent-search-trajectories width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel line chart across eight optimization rounds for five curated KernelBench operators. Panel (a) plots matrix-vector multiplication latency in milliseconds, where a dashed orange line shows non-monotonic per-round candidate latency with a sharp rise at Round 5 and a solid green step curve traces the monotonically falling lowest recorded latency. Panel (b) plots lowest recorded latency as a fraction of Round 1 across all five operators using solid step curves with markers."}

The matrix–vector search reaches `{python} ka10_mv_low_ms`\ ms in Round `{python} ka10_mv_low_round`, records `{python} ka10_mv_peak_ms`\ ms in Round `{python} ka10_mv_peak_round`, and does not beat that earlier low until Round `{python} ka10_mv_best_round`, whereas RMSNorm gains little after Round 1. Each plotted record is the one kernel the source keeps from its round's four workers, so the curves understate how far candidates strayed. The other workers' times survive only in the attempt history carried by later prompts. In every round those histories cover (Rounds 1 to `{python} ka10_hist_last_round` of each task), the plotted record is the fastest timed attempt, while the slowest attempts reach `{python} ka10_mv_worst_ms`\ ms for matrix–vector and `{python} ka10_tc_worst_ms`\ ms for the transposed convolution. One matrix–vector attempt failed verification and has no time, and Round `{python} ka10_rounds` leaves no history beyond its kept kernel. The lowest record also need not be the kernel the source finally keeps. RMSNorm's final kernel closely matches its Round `{python} ka10_rms_final_round` kernel, whereas its lowest record comes from Round `{python} ka10_rms_low_round`, `{python} ka10_rms_final_gap_pct` percent below the Round `{python} ka10_rms_final_round` record and far inside RMSNorm's own timing spread discussed below.

The figure's ratios also start from a search output rather than from the input kernel or a conventional baseline. Against `torch.compile`, the PyTorch compiler that the source uses as its baseline [@Cheng2025KernelAgentArtifacts], the matrix–vector input kernel starts `{python} ka10_mv_input_vs_compile`$\times$ slower and the search's Round 1 output is still `{python} ka10_mv_r1_vs_compile`$\times$ slower, so most of its `{python} ka10_mv_ratio`$\times$ gain recovers ground the generated kernel started behind, and its final kernel ends `{python} ka10_mv_vs_compile`$\times$ faster. RMSNorm's input kernel already runs ahead of `torch.compile`, and its final kernel ends `{python} ka10_rms_vs_compile`$\times$ faster, so the nearly flat curve hides the larger gain over that baseline. These ratios also assume correct kernels, and that correctness rests on the source's own execution-based checks with tolerances, which we did not repeat. That limit matters because @ZhangEtAl2026KernelBenchVerified report that models exploit KernelBench's narrow test distribution with hardcoded bypasses. For the best of the seven models they test, in single-turn generation at Level 1, hidden tests cut the 32-bit speedup over eager PyTorch from 1.37$\times$ to 1.17$\times$, and a baseline with Tensor Cores enabled lowers it further. In 16-bit evaluation, the precision of these traces, the same model reaches 0.90$\times$ at Level 1 and 1.63$\times$ at Level 2, and the authors attribute the Level 2 gain to operator fusion. That study tests neither KernelAgent nor `torch.compile`, so it does not show that these kernels are affected.

The figure uses only the per-round records, which disagree with the source's summary table for `{python} ka10_off_tasks` tasks. The largest gap falls on the transposed convolution, whose table values run about `{python} ka10_tc_scale`$\times$ the records in every round and so leave its ratio to Round 1 nearly unchanged. The records report a warmup setting of `{python} ka10_warmup_records` where the supplied benchmark script uses `{python} ka10_warmup_script`, so the two sets may come from different procedures, and the artifacts do not establish the cause. That gap separates two sets of numbers, whereas panel (a) compares records within one set, so it says little about noise inside the records. The source publishes no timing variance. The closest evidence is the starting times that each task's four Round 1 workers report for what the trace layout indicates is one input kernel. These small samples spread `{python} ka10_conv_start_spread`$\times$ for both convolutions, `{python} ka10_mp_start_spread`$\times$ for MaxPool, `{python} ka10_mv_start_spread`$\times$ for matrix–vector, and `{python} ka10_rms_start_spread`$\times$ for RMSNorm.

Even against the widest of those spreads, regression is common in these traces. Of the `{python} ka10_att_timed` timed attempts, `{python} ka10_att_slower` ran slower than the kernel they started from and `{python} ka10_att_faster` ran faster. Beyond the `{python} ka10_rms_start_spread`$\times$ RMSNorm spread, the count is `{python} ka10_att_slower_beyond` slower and `{python} ka10_att_faster_beyond` faster. Even the kept records, each its round's best, sit above their task's earlier low in `{python} ka10_late_above` of the `{python} ka10_late_rounds` rounds after Round 1, and `{python} ka10_late_beyond` of them exceed that spread, in every task except RMSNorm.

The matrix–vector spike in panel (a) is a less direct case. The Round `{python} ka10_mv_peak_round` record stands `{python} ka10_mv_peak_ratio`$\times$ above the earlier low, but the rounds are branches of a beam rather than a single lineage, and that record starts from a `{python} ka10_mv_parent_ms`\ ms kernel, not from the low. Its `{python} ka10_mv_parent_ratio`$\times$ step from that parent exceeds the matrix–vector spread but lies inside the RMSNorm spread, so these samples do not separate that step from noise. The two Round `{python} ka10_mv_peak_round` workers that did start from the low averaged about `{python} ka10_mv_from_low_ms`\ ms, about `{python} ka10_mv_from_low_ratio`$\times$ above it and beyond every spread. Matrix–vector's smaller rises, at most `{python} ka10_mv_other_rise`$\times$, also fall inside the widest spread, and these records cannot separate them from timing noise.

These traces, which the source curates as a demonstration, are not a representative sample of KernelBench [@OuyangEtAl2025KernelBench] and do not establish a general speedup distribution, but they show why the lowest recorded time cannot stand in for the history of candidates. In our NPU study, the same distinction means retaining the centralized candidate's reports even if a later banked revision performs better. A candidate's failure may explain the next proposal; overwriting that run would erase the reason for the change.

### Stage 3: Implementing Testable Hardware and Software

The wider centralized candidate now needs hardware, software, and verification inputs that tools can execute together. Stage 3 (Implement) produces transaction-level models that simulate its data movement as whole transfers rather than individual signals, synthesizable RTL for the crossbar and accumulator datapaths, and a software schedule that supplies the intended parallel work. A wider datapath offers little benefit if the compiled schedule still feeds it at the baseline rate, and a build against stale transaction models may test a different design altogether. To keep generation and verification independent (@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales), the team checks the candidate against requirements fixed before it was generated, such as formal properties or a reference model. Only then does it spend downstream tool budget.

Building those hardware and software artifacts is only half of implementation; the study also has to run them through tools that match the fidelity of the question. An early behavioral model is enough to test an algorithm or tiling schedule, whereas estimating physical timing requires synthesizable RTL and calibrated electrical models; @sec-data-representations-world-models develops these representation choices. Tool runtime then limits how many candidates a team can run through physical implementation at once, and in a commercial flow electronic design automation (EDA) license counts add a second limit, although this chapter retains no license record from such a flow.

Check cost rises from linting and functional simulation to synthesis and place-and-route, and even the one small open-flow design retained in @fig-ch06-implementation-stage-costs spends more of its run in detailed routing than in any other step. The team therefore screens candidates in tiers (@sec-signal-sources-attrition), treating each early check as a filter rather than a signoff certificate. Passing a behavioral simulation justifies running synthesis on a candidate, but says nothing about whether the resulting layout will satisfy the foundry's physical design rules.[^fn-drc-c03]

[^fn-drc-c03]: **Design rule checking (DRC)**: A check of layout geometry against a semiconductor foundry's manufacturing rules, such as minimum wire widths and spacing. Passing establishes compliance with the rules checked rather than guaranteed fabrication yield, and behavioral simulation never tests these geometric limits.

Even before physical checks begin, implementation has to verify that the tools actually tested the intended design. A syntactically clean script can still point to the wrong top-level module, hold an active-low reset asserted throughout simulation, or skip the target workload phase. Similarly, a generated RTL block can pass its unit testbench while violating an interconnect handshake or compiling against a mismatched software target. The execution harness, the coordinator that dispatches each tool run and binds its outcome to the candidate, is meant to catch those silent mismatches by keeping the candidate hardware, supporting software, interface assertions, and tool inputs tied together throughout the run.

When a tool run fails outright, the harness must also separate operational faults from bad hardware before feeding the outcome back into search. A license checkout timeout says nothing about circuit timing, and a host out-of-memory kill might reflect a cramped container limit, a tool bug, or a genuinely unroutable netlist. Tracking those distinctions across automated retries is the job of the tool interfaces and run management developed in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces. Once a run completes cleanly, Stage 4 (Evaluate) asks what the returned measurements actually establish about the design.

### Stage 4: Evaluating Candidates with Simulators and Tools

Once implementation confirms that the intended design and workload actually ran, evaluation judges whether the results of the checks run during Implement answer the planned question. A clean tool exit alone does not make a measurement valid. Because cycle-level simulators can overrate designs whose delay is dominated by global wiring, establishing the NPU candidate's physical and functional feasibility requires checks that observe those limits directly, such as static timing analysis (STA),[^fn-sta-c03] design rule checking (DRC), logic equivalence checking, clock-domain crossing checks, and dynamic voltage-drop ($IR$-drop) analysis. Any study that stops short of those checks must keep its conclusions within the models it actually ran.

In our walkthrough, suppose the implemented centralized candidate compiles cleanly and the cycle simulator predicts higher accumulator throughput at the target clock frequency. STA then reports a setup timing violation on the accumulator paths while power-integrity analysis flags localized $IR$ drop near critical buffers.[^fn-ir-drop-c03] Evaluation records that the design fails its declared timing constraint. Because the simulated throughput gain assumes a clock frequency that the physical layout cannot sustain, the candidate cannot be accepted as an improvement.

[^fn-sta-c03]: **Static timing analysis (STA)**: The timing check introduced with logic synthesis in @sec-moonshot. A setup timing violation indicates negative slack, meaning data arrives too late relative to the clock edge and the circuit cannot reliably operate at the target clock frequency.

[^fn-ir-drop-c03]: **IR drop**: A voltage decrease caused by current flowing through resistance in the power-distribution network. Reduced supply voltage can slow switching and contribute to timing violations.

Evaluation records each requirement separately as passed, failed, or unresolved, so a passing functional test does not mask a timing violation and an unmeasured power budget remains marked as unknown. The localized voltage drop offers an initial clue to why the paths slowed down, but finding the physical cause is the job of Interpret.

### Stage 5: Interpreting What the Measurements Show

Knowing which checks passed or failed does not by itself tell the team what to change next. The centralized accumulator's timing violation could arise from long crossbar wires, inadequate power delivery, weak buffers, or an improperly configured timing constraint. Stage 5 (Interpret) asks which explanation the evidence supports and what test would distinguish the remaining possibilities. Tools can help extract the failing paths, separate cell delay from net delay, and propose explanations, but a plausible account is still a hypothesis until tested.[^fn-credit-assignment-c03]

Suppose the path reports suggest that long shared interconnect dominates the delay. The team can test that explanation by returning to Implement and Evaluate for a controlled comparison, such as a shorter interconnect path under the same clock, operating conditions, and analysis settings. The comparison must also account for changes in buffering, placement, or capacitive load that could explain the result. These diagnostic runs consume budget just as candidate evaluations do; the study plan must allow for them rather than treating troubleshooting as free work.

The diagnosis guides the choice between local and structural repair. If cell delay is substantial, gate sizing or lower-threshold-voltage ($V_t$) cells may improve timing, but faster cells can also increase leakage. A local timing repair can therefore exhaust the block's power allocation within the subsystem's 3\ W envelope. If wire delay remains dominant, further cell changes may buy little, giving the team a reason to reconsider the centralized organization. Neither failed local repairs nor a single path report proves that banking will succeed.

If the diagnostic comparison supports the wire-delay explanation, the next iteration returns to Explore to develop the banked alternative, then to Implement for distributed accumulators, local reduction trees, and a matching software schedule. Evaluate must check this revision's numerical behavior, timing, and power under the original requirements; shorter wires may help timing while bank conflicts or extra reduction stages reduce the expected throughput gain. A Layer 3 system authorized to revise the internal organization could carry this sequence forward automatically. A Layer 2 optimizer could do so only if banking and its matching schedule were already encoded in its template; otherwise the proposal returns to the architect. In either case, a repair that changes the external bus contract or block power allocation requires reopening Formulate.

The failed centralized candidate remains part of the record, the banked revision becomes a new candidate, and its results may support or challenge the diagnosis. Because the walkthrough is constructed and that revision never ran, it shows where the loop would close without closing it. The verification and feedback methods in @sec-feedback-verification-trust develop these checks further.

[^fn-credit-assignment-c03]: **The architectural credit assignment problem**: In multi-stage closed-loop design, attributing a downstream physical failure (such as negative slack, routing congestion, or localized $IR$ drop) to an upstream design decision is, by analogy, a classic credit assignment challenge [@Minsky1961StepsAI]. Sensitivity analysis and controlled counterfactual trials can help distinguish competing causes before triggering expensive structural redesigns.

When the available runs cannot distinguish competing explanations, the study retains them and either requests further diagnostic runs or moves to Commit for review. A clear account of what remains unresolved is a useful engineering outcome alongside a supported design recommendation.

### Stage 6: Reviewing the Evidence and Making a Decision

Without an explicit review step at the end of a study, an automated loop can promote a block whose local speedup shifts memory traffic and thermal load onto neighboring SoC blocks, or mistake an exhausted run budget for proof that a target is infeasible. Commit is meant to catch both errors. It ends the study with a reviewed decision about what the completed work justifies doing next: advancing a candidate, rejecting it, revising the question, or stopping with unresolved issues.

Because the stakes depend on the study's scope, advancing a revised NPU block to subsystem integration carries different obligations from approving a full chip for mask freeze.[^fn-mask-freeze-c03] When a revised NPU block satisfies its declared checks, the responsible architect reviews the hardware and software changes, the comparison conditions, the physical explanation for the speedup, and the remaining system-level limitations before recommending integration. If timing still fails or the run budget runs out, the architect can authorize another study or record that the bounded search ended without a winner, rather than waive the failing check to reach a milestone.

[^fn-mask-freeze-c03]: **Mask freeze**: The final signoff milestone (often termed tapeout) where physical layout geometries are locked and released to manufacture optical lithography reticles (photomasks). Unlike a software patch, a silicon defect found after mask freeze generally requires new masks and a respin, which at advanced process nodes is among the most expensive and time-consuming corrections a program can make.

::: {.callout-law title="Normalization of Deviance in Verification Waivers"}
**The Classical Principle:** Technical deviations can come to be accepted as normal when repeated exposure produces no immediate failure, so that the absence of failure stands in for a justification [@Vaughan1996Challenger].

**The Hardware Trap:** By analogy, an automated loop that cannot close a formal proof or a clock-domain-crossing check leaves warnings behind, and schedule pressure invites waiving them. Because a waived path may never fail at nominal voltage and temperature, each accepted waiver can make the next one easier, and an unverified race condition can then appear in silicon at an operating extreme.

**The Architectural Antidote:** Route each waiver to Commit as a decision with a technical rationale, a named owner, and a condition for reopening it, and keep the loop's constraint files read-only to it (@sec-what-architect-owns; @sec-law-normalization-deviance in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

Routine implementation and tuning iterations proceed automatically inside the scope and budget set during Formulate, while human review is reserved for when a candidate meets the planned decision criteria, when a repair requires changing the study's scope, or when a stopping condition triggers.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="From the NPU block to the Lighthouse subsystem"}
**Context.** The accumulator study examines one block in a candidate Lighthouse design. Its results must eventually be evaluated in the XR workload that motivated the design.

**Application.** Faster accumulation may shorten a workload stage, but additional transfers or memory contention may erase that gain. The integrated comparison must check workload deadlines, the matching software schedule, and power across the subsystem, including memory and leakage.

**Outcome.** A successful block study could justify evaluating the revised NPU in the surrounding system. Whether that Lighthouse candidate meets its 3\ W target and real-time requirements remains a question for the subsystem study.
:::

Together, the six stages serve as a practical reference for planning and reviewing a study, keeping their starting inputs, deliverables, and return conditions distinct even when one engineer or tool performs several activities (@tbl-stage-seams).

| **Stage** | **Starts from** | **Produces** | **Reason to revisit** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Formulate** | Product goals and system requirements. | A question, baseline, scope, checks, and stopping conditions. | Evidence calls the target, assumptions, or permitted changes into question. |
| **Explore** | The plan and what earlier candidates taught. | Candidate organizations or configurations, with reasons for testing them. | A candidate fails, or a result suggests a better alternative. |
| **Implement** | A candidate and the checks it needs. | Testable hardware and software, tool inputs, and execution results. | Artifacts need revision, or the intended checks did not run. |
| **Evaluate** | Execution results and the planned comparison. | Valid comparisons and passed, failed, or unresolved checks. | Conditions are mismatched or observations are insufficient. |
| **Interpret** | Checked results and possible explanations. | Supported explanations, remaining hypotheses, and proposed investigations. | Causes remain uncertain or another result contradicts the explanation. |
| **Commit** | The plan, comparisons, explanations, and limitations. | A reviewed decision to advance, reject, revise, or stop. | Missing evidence or a changed requirement reopens the decision. |
: **Inputs, outputs, and return conditions across the six life-cycle stages.** Each stage owns a distinct engineering deliverable and reopens when downstream measurements invalidate its starting assumptions or artifacts. {#tbl-stage-seams tbl-colwidths="[15,25,30,30]"}

No stage operates on the output of its immediate predecessor alone (@tbl-stage-seams). Evaluate compares results from Implement against the criteria fixed in Formulate, while Interpret may request a new implementation to test a suspected cause. Commit weighs the baseline, failed trials, explanations, and remaining uncertainties rather than only the final run. Another architect must be able to follow these connections to understand why the team selected a repair or stopped the study, even when automated search performed the intervening iterations.

## Recording the Loop in a Study Record {#sec-design-loop-card}

Reviewing the NPU study requires more than its best timing report. Another architect needs to know which candidate produced that report, which workload and constraints applied, why the candidate was selected, and what earlier failures taught the team. Much of this information already sits in repositories, experiment logs, and verification reports, but scattered files do not explain a design choice until they are connected to the original question and the resulting decision.

A *study record* links the initial plan, candidate revisions, comparisons, explanations, and failed or unfinished runs to the decision or stopping reason (@fig-structured-layer-above-rtl). An *execution record* captures a single tool attempt, including its inputs, tool conditions, diagnostic outputs, and completion status. In the constructed NPU example, an execution record would retain the centralized accumulator's timing violation, while the study record would explain how that failure led to testing a banked revision. Both are needed to distinguish a new design from a retry of the same run and to preserve what earlier failures taught the team.

> **Design-loop card.** A short structured index for the study record, with study-plan fields fixed before any tool runs: the scoped study's baseline, candidate space, execution budget, verification criteria, and reviewer. As the study proceeds, execution records are linked to the plan and findings are appended. It borrows contextual documentation from Model Cards and Datasheets for Datasets [@MitchellEtAl2019ModelCards; @GebruEtAl2021Datasheets] and points into existing engineering records rather than replacing them.

![**A scoped architecture study links high-level design judgment to low-level tool execution.** Top-level design intent, analytical models, and system requirements feed into a bounded study record that tracks the question under review, linked artifacts, and supported findings. Below it, outputs from simulators, compilers, RTL generators, and EDA signoff engines return along a common path to either support an architectural decision or trigger a claim revision.](images/fig-structured-layer-above-rtl){#fig-structured-layer-above-rtl width="72%" fig-alt="Diagram in which system intent and human judgment appear above a scoped architecture study, which links its question and artifacts to results from implementation tools below. Feedback connects the study to further design work and review."}

Those links connect a cycle count to the workload trace and simulator configuration that produced it, or a timing estimate to its PVT corners, cell libraries, and clock constraints in Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) files.[^fn-sdc-c03] A reviewer can then determine what a reported gain rests on and which comparisons need to be rerun when an upstream assumption changes. The card indexes these engineering records; it need not duplicate their contents.

[^fn-sdc-c03]: **Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC)**: A format for specifying clocks, input and output delays, timing exceptions, and related constraints used by synthesis and timing-analysis tools.

Alongside the NPU investigation, consider the prospective study that later chapters follow, a comparison of a 2\ MiB level-2 (L2) cache baseline against 3\ MiB and 4\ MiB alternatives, with the workload, software, cache policies, and surrounding architecture held fixed. The question is whether fewer capacity misses reduce 99th-percentile frame time on the selected XRBench workload [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench] while meeting cache area and access-time limits and the subsystem's 3\ W power budget. A direct comparison of these capacities needs no learned optimizer. It still needs a study record to connect the planned comparison to what the tools eventually establish.

A cycle-level simulator would measure frame times, while a static random-access memory (SRAM) model[^fn-sram-model-c03] would estimate array area, access latency, and power. The subsystem power check must also include the NPU and surrounding blocks. The card in @fig-filled-design-loop-card links these different tool outputs to the same candidate and workload and names the reviewer responsible for the decision. A CACTI screen of the three capacities has run at 22\ nm (@sec-mobile-xr-evaluation), and every area it returned exceeds the planned limit, but those returns describe a different process and cannot answer the target-node question. The card's findings therefore remain open, because the target-node comparison is a plan, not a completed execution.

[^fn-sram-model-c03]: **SRAM models**: Dense multi-megabyte cache arrays use custom analog-digital bitcells and sense amplifiers that cannot be efficiently synthesized from standard logic gates. Architectural exploration relies on analytical tools (such as CACTI [@MuralimanoharEtAl2009CACTI]) or foundry memory compilers to evaluate area, access latency, dynamic power, and static leakage for specific banking configurations.

![**A pre-committed design-loop card separates the study plan from its eventual outcome.** For the prospective Lighthouse L2 cache sweep (2, 3, and 4\ MiB), twelve fields record the claim under review, workload state, direct-enumeration method, tool budget, and responsible reviewer before execution begins. Findings and decisions later record completed checks, failures, and unresolved limits.](images/fig-filled-design-loop-card){#fig-filled-design-loop-card width="75%" fig-alt="Illustration of a study card for a prospective XR cache study. A hypothesis precedes entries for the baseline, candidates, checks, execution budget, evidence needed, and responsible reviewer. No completed result is reported."}

The planned budget in @fig-filled-design-loop-card permits at most four cycle-level runs, including reruns, plus one SRAM screening evaluation per capacity. If those observations cannot separate a candidate's gain from the sampling uncertainty of a 99th-percentile frame time measured over a finite trace, the record must preserve an unresolved outcome or an explicitly revised plan. The lowest observed frame time alone does not justify selecting a winner.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Stop when the tools cannot observe the target"}
**The principle:** A valid architectural outcome includes rejecting every candidate, retaining the baseline reference, or halting exploration before tool dispatch when the available tools cannot observe the physical property in question.

**The application:** An analytical memory model such as CACTI derives its estimates from generic technology parameters rather than a foundry's qualified bitcells, multi-threshold leakage distributions, or write-assist circuits, and the pinned CACTI 7 run in @sec-mobile-xr-evaluation supports nodes only down to 22\ nm. It therefore cannot evaluate a leading-edge node such as TSMC N3E, so any figure at that node would be an extrapolation or would have to come from a foundry memory compiler. When evaluation prerequisites or calibrated tool collateral are missing, an AI-native design system should stop before dispatch, or label the returns as uncalibrated, rather than treat them as measurements. Stopping there is a valid outcome of the study, and its record should state what was missing.
:::

Separate records also make dependencies between studies visible. If the team later adopts a banked NPU accumulator, changes in interconnect traffic, heat dissipation, or background power may invalidate the cache study's baseline. The architect can then reopen the affected comparisons while retaining results whose assumptions still hold. If the cache study instead reveals a bottleneck that capacity changes cannot address, a proposal to revise the interconnect or software data layout returns to Formulate for a broader study that carries this negative evidence forward. The record keeps the two cases apart: comparisons reopened because their assumptions changed, and findings that motivate a new question.

Carrying out and reviewing these studies in practice takes the four technical building blocks developed in the next part of this book: structured representations for designs and constraints (@sec-data-representations-world-models), method selection matched to the bottleneck and run budget (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization), reproducible tool harnesses (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces), and verification checks that test tool outputs before they drive a design change (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). Each building block serves several life-cycle stages rather than mapping to the six stages one for one.

## Open Questions

Breaking the design loop into six explicit stages clarifies what each handoff must record, but it also exposes four hard research problems that arise when teams try to automate those handoffs across real hardware tools:

- **How do we filter out weak candidates early without throwing away hardware designs that only work once the compiler schedule and physical layout are tuned to match them?** Running candidates step by step through behavioral simulation, logic synthesis, and place-and-route saves scarce EDA licenses, but strict early cutoffs can reject a promising distributed accumulator simply because it was tested with a compiler schedule built for a centralized crossbar. Yet the opposite approach, tuning a custom compiler schedule and running physical placement for every proposed block, quickly burns the study's compute budget on designs that fail basic functional or area checks. We still lack multi-stage screening rules that can bound the risk of rejecting a good hardware organization before its software and physical layout have had a chance to adapt.

- **When a post-route signoff check fails, how can an automated workflow tell which earlier stage caused the problem?** When STA signoff fails in a 3\ nm flow, the tool reports a failing gate-level path through extracted wire parasitics. That single violation could come from an unrealistic clock target set in Formulate, a centralized crossbar chosen in Explore, unpipelined RTL written in Implement, or random variation in the placement seed. An architect or automated loop cannot afford to rerun full place-and-route to test every possible explanation, yet blaming wire-dominated delay on local gate sizing will trap a Layer 2 optimizer in pointless $V_t$ swaps. We need diagnostic methods that can pinpoint which upstream stage broke the design using only a handful of targeted tool runs.

- **When an optimizer fails to find a working design, how do we tell whether the search simply ran out of budget or the hardware template itself cannot meet the target?** Suppose a Layer 2 optimizer repeatedly fails to close timing on the NPU accumulator without exceeding the block's leakage allocation within the subsystem's 3\ W envelope. Those failed runs alone do not prove that no valid parameter setting $\theta$ exists inside the fixed hardware template $\Theta$. If the template truly has no working point, running more parameter sweeps wastes compute. If a valid point is still hiding in the space, reopening Formulate too early to relax the clock target or change bus interfaces excuses a weak search algorithm. We still lack reliable tests that combine physical scaling limits, calibrated surrogate uncertainty, and formal infeasibility bounds to tell an architect when to stop tuning parameters and change the hardware organization.

- **How can separate block-level studies share power, thermal, and bandwidth budgets without forcing the team to optimize the entire SoC at once?** Scoped design-loop cards keep each block's failure modes easy to inspect, but neighboring blocks still share physical budgets: adopting a faster banked NPU accumulator can change interconnect traffic and heat dissipation enough to invalidate a companion L2 cache study inside the same 3\ W envelope. No team can afford to rerun cycle-accurate simulation and full place-and-route across the whole subsystem after every block edit, yet rigid upfront budgets for each block miss cross-block trade-offs. Hardware design loops need ways to pass power, thermal, and bandwidth sensitivities between sibling study cards and flag when two coupled blocks must be optimized together.

## Summary

Whether a team runs a simple parameter sweep or wrestles with those open research problems, the six-stage life cycle connects an architecture question to candidate proposals, testable implementation, valid measurement, causal diagnosis, and a reviewed decision. Our constructed NPU walkthrough follows a centralized candidate from a promising throughput estimate to a physical timing failure, then uses diagnostic tests to motivate a banked revision. That revision still has to be built and checked before an architect can decide whether it should advance.

This shared structure gives the rest of the book a common backbone while leaving room for very different levels of automation. A three-point L2 cache comparison can evaluate every candidate by hand, whereas a broader AI-native study may generate and test new hardware and software organizations automatically. Both studies still require fair comparisons, recorded tool conditions, and an explicit account of what the evidence actually supports. Changing how much of the loop is automated never removes those engineering obligations.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Begin with a testable question.** The baseline, requirements, permitted changes, and stopping conditions make later comparisons meaningful while leaving room for alternative organizations.
- **Connect generation to implementation.** A proposed organization needs a representation that can express it, along with matching hardware, software, and checks before its benefits can be assessed.
- **Separate evaluation from interpretation.** Establish what passed, failed, or remains unknown, then investigate why and use the findings to guide another design.
- **Revisit the work affected by a result.** Preserve earlier results whose assumptions still hold, and investigate coupled causes before selecting a repair.
- **Keep the decision proportional to the evidence.** Retain the conditions, failed attempts, and limitations needed for review. Advancing, rejecting, revising, and stopping with the question unresolved are all legitimate outcomes, and exhausting a run budget ends the permitted search without proving the target infeasible.
:::

Before any method can propose or compare alternatives like the centralized and banked NPU accumulators, however, it needs a concrete way to encode hardware organizations, workloads, and physical constraints. Turning those design artifacts and tool outputs into machine-usable state is the task of @sec-data-representations-world-models, starting with the architectural data from which every representation and predictive model is built.
